This means admins who set a tighter limit (e.g. 3 MB) will accept up to 10 MB in the browser, only to be rejected by the server (or worse, accepted via the new auto-downsize path on the server). If the input is much bigger than `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` (e.g. 20 MB uploaded against a 1 MB limit) the loop exits with `attempt == 0` and `tempfile.size` still > the limit. `Upload.create_for` is then called with an oversized file, which either fails with a confusing error or, if server-side validation is lenient, succeeds with a file violating the configured policy. The loop should compare the actual byte size to the limit and either grow the reduction factor, use binary search on the quality/scale, or surface a clear error when the target cannot be reached."

On installations with a tight policy, a remote URL can now fetch up to 10 MB and then attempt to downsize; on installations that set a higher limit, downloads above the configured limit are still capped at 10 MB. Any future caller that forwards user-controlled content into `dimensions` (or into `from`/`to` paths) can inject shell metacharacters and achieve command execution as the Rails process. The code should use the array form (e.g. `system(*instructions, out: '/dev/null', err: '/dev/null')`) so each argument is passed directly to `execve` without a shell."

The comment also conflates pixel-dimension reduction with byte-size reduction, which can mislead future maintainers.
